# CHAPTER X

POLITICAL MORALITY (1862)

On Moran's promotion to be Secretary, Mr. Seward inquired whether Minister Adams would like the place of Assistant Secretary for his son. It was the first—and last—office ever offered him, if indeed he could claim what was offered to his father. To them both, the change seemed useless. More than half his duties were domestic and always required independence of the Government service. Any young man could make some sort of Assistant Secretary; only one, just at that moment, could make an Assistant Son. His position was abnormal. The British Government by courtesy allowed the son to go to Court as Attaché, though he was never attached. In the Legation he was liable to do Secretary's work; in society, when unofficial, he was a young man without any position at all. Gradually he aspired to become a gentleman, just a member of society like the rest. The position was irregular; yet it lent itself to a sort of irregular education that seemed to be the only sort of education the young man was ever to get.

Such as it was, few young men had more. The spring and summer of 1863 saw a great change in Secretary Seward's management of foreign affairs. Under the stimulus of danger, he too got education. In order to affect European opinion, the weight of American opinion had to be brought to bear personally, and Seward set vigorously to work and sent over every important American on whom he could lay his hands.

The most interesting was Thurlow Weed, who took charge of the press, and began, to the amused astonishment of the secretaries, by making what the Legation had learned to accept as the invariable mistake of every amateur diplomat: he wrote letters to the London *Times*. Mistake or not, Mr. Weed soon got into his hands the threads of management, and did quietly and smoothly all that was to be done. Thurlow Weed was a complete American education in himself. His mind was naturally strong and beautifully balanced; his manners were carefully perfect in the style of benevolent simplicity, the tradition of Benjamin Franklin. Of all flowers in the garden of education, confidence was becoming the rarest; but before Mr. Weed went away, young Adams followed him about much like a little dog.

The trait that astounded and confounded cynicism was his apparent unselfishness. The effect of power on all men is the aggravation of self, a sort of tumor that ends by killing the victim's sympathies; and Thurlow Weed was a rare immune. He thought apparently not of himself, but of the person he was talking with. He grasped power, but not office. He distributed offices by handfuls without caring to take them. He had the instinct of empire: he gave, but he did not receive. Management was an instinct with him; an object to be pursued for its own sake, as one plays cards; but he appeared to play with men as though they were only cards. Once, when he had told some stories of his political experience which were strong even for the Albany lobby, the private secretary made bold to ask him outright: "Then, Mr. Weed, do you think that no politician can be trusted?" Mr. Weed hesitated for a moment; then said in his mild manner: "I never advise a young man to begin by thinking so."

The lesson, at the time, translated itself in a moral sense, as though Mr. Weed had said: "Youth needs illusions!" As he grew older he rather thought that Mr. Weed looked on it as a question of how the game should be played. Principles had better be left aside; values were enough. Secretary Seward also sent William M. Evarts to London as law counsel. Evarts was as individual as Weed was impersonal; he played the game in a large and liberal way, "a great advocate employed in politics," and was an economist of morals: "The world can absorb only doses of truth," he said; "too much would kill it." One sought education in order to adjust the dose.

England's power of absorbing truth was small. Englishmen such as Palmerston, Russell, Bethell, and the society represented by the *Times*, as well as the Tories represented by Disraeli and the *Standard*, offered a study that sickened a young student with anxiety. He had begun—contrary to Mr. Weed's advice—by taking their bad faith for granted. To settle this point became the main object of his diplomatic education. Life changed front, according as one thought one's self dealing with honest men or with rogues.

The recognition of belligerency, the Declaration of Paris, the Trent Affair, all strengthened the belief that Lord Russell had started in May, 1861, with the assumption that the Confederacy was established; he was waiting only for the proper moment to interpose. All these points seemed self-evident—except that Lord Russell obstinately denied the whole charge, and persisted in assuring Minister Adams of his honest and impartial neutrality.

With the insolence of youth, Henry Adams jumped to the conclusion that Earl Russell lied; and, although the Minister thought differently, he had to act as though Russell were false. The most costly tutors in the world were provided for him at public expense—Palmerston, Russell, Westbury, Selborne, Gladstone, Granville—paid by the British Government; Seward, Charles Francis Adams, Evarts, Weed, paid by the American. There was only one student to profit by this immense staff of teachers.

Never was demonstration more tangled. Hegel's metaphysical doctrine of the identity of opposites was simpler. The stages began in June, 1862, with remonstrances against the escape of "No. 290." Lord Russell declined to act on the evidence. On July 24, Collier's legal opinion was sent: "It appears difficult to make out a stronger case of infringement of the Foreign Enlistment Act, which, if not enforced on this occasion, is little better than a dead letter." In spite of the warning, Earl Russell let the ship, four days afterwards, escape.

If one could not trust a dozen of the most respected private characters in the world, composing the Queen's Ministry, one could trust no mortal man. Lord Russell felt the force of this inference, and undertook to disprove it. His effort lasted till his death. At first he excused himself by throwing the blame on the law officers; then he pleaded guilty to criminal negligence, and said in his *Recollections*: "I assent entirely to the opinion of the Lord Chief Justice of England that the Alabama ought to have been detained during the four days I was waiting for the opinion of the law officers... it was my fault as Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs." Of course it was his fault! The true issue lay not in the question of his fault, but of his intent. There could be no sense in history unless a constant course of faults implied a constant motive.

Minister Adams held the convenient belief that, in the main, Russell was true, and died still holding it. His son wanted to know whether he could, in politics, risk trusting any one. Russell alone insisted on his honesty of intention and persuaded both the Duke of Argyll and the Minister to believe him. They knew he expected the rebels to win in the end, but believed he would not actively interpose. On that—on nothing else—they rested their frail hopes of remaining a day longer in England.

In 1889, Spencer Walpole published the official life of Earl Russell, and told a part of the story which had never been known to the Minister and which astounded his son. The Alabama escaped, by Russell's confessed negligence, on July 28, 1862. In America the Union armies had suffered great disasters before Richmond and at the second Bull Run, followed by Lee's invasion of Maryland, the news of which, arriving in England on September 14, roused the idea that the crisis was at hand. Palmerston instantly wrote to Russell: "If this should happen, would it not be time for us to consider whether in such a state of things England and France might not address the contending parties and recommend an arrangement on the basis of separation?"

Forty years later, Gladstone's own confession revealed that the Cabinet's drift toward intervention had been even nearer success than Adams had supposed; the lesson stood, that in politics no professed friend in power could be trusted, and that the diplomatic victory of 1862 had been won against men who scarcely knew their own minds.
